title: Redwood technical deep dive: OOMs, timeouts, CUDA, retry semantics
summary: Deep dive with HelixMed on recurring OOMs and timeouts when running 70B models on Dedicated GPUs. Discussed root causes (batching, KV cache pressure, CUDA OOMs, fragmentation), retry semantics, timeout tuning, and mitigations (batch caps, quantization, pinned memory, GC knobs, graceful fallbacks). Agreed next steps: share logs, run repro with stress script, try 4-bit quant profile, and schedule a follow-up benchmark next week.
action_items: Ethan: run stress repro on HelixMed test env and attach detailed allocator logs - due 2026-03-30
HelixMed (Raj): share pod logs + gpu-smi snapshots from last 5 incidents in private S3 - due 2026-03-29
Oliver: prepare recommended config (batch caps, kv cache size, retry backoff) for 70B model - due 2026-03-31
Maya: share Redwood stability checklist and security docs, include link to bench spreadsheet - due 2026-03-28
next_steps: Send repro harness and instructions via email
Run quantized 4-bit profile on dedicated pool during maintenance window
Schedule follow-up benchmark session (45m) next Tue 10am PT
Set up temporary increased logging for allocator + RPC timeouts
transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. we know this has been painful, so we want to walk through the OOMs and timeouts you saw with the 70B and talk through mitigations.
[00:00:12] Sarah Lawson: thanks Maya, yeah the incidents spike last week when traffic hit ~120 qps, we saw a bunch of pod restarts and some requests timing out > 30s.
[00:00:25] Ethan Park: ok, quick clarification, are these Dedicated GPUs or Private on-prem?
[00:00:29] Raj Patel: Dedicated in our VPC; Redwood Dedicated pool, but network path is via our VPC peering.
[00:00:34] Oliver Reyes: got it. first suspicion is memory pressure from KV cache + batching. with 70B the KV cache per token can be sizable and if batching spikes you can exceed device memory.
[00:00:48] Tom Wu: we saw cuda OOMs in the kernel logs, sometimes immediately before a timeout. logs show "CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY" and then the process retries.
[00:00:57] Ethan Park: ok, two separate issues: 1) transient OOMs at kernel allocation time, and 2) timeouts from upper layer when retries/backoff not tuned. both can cascade.
[00:01:10] Sarah Lawson: sometimes the OOMs happen mid-stream, like after a 200-token generation. is that fragmentation?
[00:01:15] Oliver Reyes: could be. GPU memory fragmentation and pinned allocations from CUDA can make a big difference. also if your batch size distribution has heavy tails, a single large request can push the allocator over.
[00:01:30] Raj Patel: we're running batching with auto-batcher and a max_batch of 16, but average batch is 8. our p95 seq len is ~350 tokens.
[00:01:40] Ethan Park: with p95 350 and 70B model, pager: that can blow up. rough rule: lower max_batch and enforce per-request token cap. also KV cache size grows with seq length; consider prefix caching for repeated prompts.
[00:01:55] Maya Chen: to be specific, we usually recommend capping batches for bigger models. for 70B, an empiric starting point is max_batch 4-8 depending on GPU type.
[00:02:06] Elena Gomez: we're on A100 80GB. thought that would be safe for 70B but clearly not if caching and bfloat allocations are high.
[00:02:14] Oliver Reyes: A100 80GB helps, but memory footprint varies with tensor parallelism, kv cache, and transient workspace. also kernel variants (fused attention) can use extra workspace.
[00:02:25] Tom Wu: question on quantization: would 4-bit quant reduce OOMs enough to keep these peaks from happening?
[00:02:30] Ethan Park: yes, 4-bit or q4_0/q4_1 profiles often reduce model weights by ~2-4x, but runtime memory (KV + workspace) still exists; quant reduces parameter memory but not always mutable workspace. you'll likely see a significant drop in peak memory but need to benchmark.
[00:02:46] Raj Patel: we tried q8 last month but saw slightly worse latency for small sequences. any tips?
[00:02:50] Oliver Reyes: that tracks — some quant kernels trade latency for memory. for low latency small seqs, mixed strategy: keep FP16 for short requests, enable quant for long-context heavy batches or background workloads. Redwood runtime supports model variants and automatic fallback.
[00:03:05] Sarah Lawson: about retries: when the runtime hits an OOM we saw a retry that lasts ~20s then times out. what's Redwood's retry semantic?
[00:03:13] Maya Chen: current default is a single retry with exponential backoff up to X seconds (configurable). We avoid immediate endless retries because that just amplifies pressure. You can tune the number of retries and backoff in the route config.
[00:03:27] Ethan Park: important detail: the retry path can be configured to fall back to a smaller model variant (e.g., 7B/13B) if the 70B fails. that's what we call graceful degradation. but for your use case, quality matters, so we should be careful.
[00:03:40] Raj Patel: can we change retry to fail fast instead of retrying? sometimes the customers prefer quick failure so they can route to a cached response.
[00:03:45] Maya Chen: yes, you can set retries=0 and short timeouts, or set a custom fallback to cached outputs. we can show exact route configs.
[00:03:55] [00:04:00] Elena Gomez: we've also seen "cuda launch timeout" in a few logs, especially when node is under multi-tenant load. is that the GPU watchdog?
[00:04:07] Oliver Reyes: sounds like it. on some cloud instances the driver will kill long-running kernels if the OS thinks it's unresponsive. that's typically seen with local display drivers but can happen in certain host configs. for Dedicated we run driver settings optimized for compute — we'll check if your pool got a misconfiguration.
[00:04:22] Tom Wu: our infra team mentioned some pods are pinned to GPUs via device plugin. could that cause subtle allocation differences?
[00:04:29] Ethan Park: pinning shouldn't cause OOMs by itself, but if a pod holds onto allocations between requests (e.g., caches not freed), fragmentation increases. we recommend periodic worker restarts or allocator tuning.
[00:04:40] Sarah Lawson: what about KV cache eviction? we saw growth until eviction kicked in and then a fallback which increased latency. any control knobs?
[00:04:47] Oliver Reyes: yes, Redwood runtime exposes kv_cache_size and eviction policy (LRU). you can set a soft limit to trigger eviction earlier. also prefix-level caching and shared cache across similar prompts reduces duplication.
[00:05:02] Raj Patel: do we lose context if KV evicts mid-generation?
[00:05:06] Ethan Park: eviction applies between requests; during a single generation we keep the necessary cache. but if a follow-up relies on evicted KV, you'll need to rewarm the cache. if rewarming is expensive, consider sticky sessions or request pinning to a warmer instance.
[00:05:20] Maya Chen: another pragmatic mitigation is to implement request shaping at the ingress: rate limit large sequences and queue them to a slower pool or dedicated quantized pool.
[00:05:30] Sarah Lawson: sounds like we need a two-pool strategy: one for low-latency small seqs on FP16, one for high-context long seqs on quantized or larger memory.
[00:05:36] Oliver Reyes: exactly. Redwood Dedicated supports routing rules by request metadata, so you can send based on sequence length or customer tier.
[00:05:44] Raj Patel: about memory fragmentation, are there recommended GC or allocator flags for CUDA?
[00:05:48] Ethan Park: yes — use cudaMallocAsync/allocator if available, and enable caching allocator tuning. For PyTorch-based runtimes, there are env vars and torch.cuda.memory_reserved tuning; for our runtime we have options to enable async alloc and free which helps reduce fragmentation. we'll share recommended flags.
[00:06:02] Tom Wu: should we bump RPC timeouts as a short-term fix?
[00:06:05] Maya Chen: careful — increasing RPC timeouts hides the symptom and can increase concurrency and memory pressure. Better to reduce concurrency per worker and tune retries.
[00:06:15] Elena Gomez: what's the impact of increasing per-worker concurrency cap vs adding more workers?
[00:06:20] Oliver Reyes: increasing workers spreads load but costs more. Lowering concurrency per worker reduces worst-case peak memory per process. Redwood autoscaling can add workers automatically when queue grows, but there's a scaling time. combining both is ideal: lower per-worker concurrency + autoscale threshold tuned to start earlier.
[00:06:36] [00:06:40] Raj Patel: small tangent: we saw occasional mis-identified labels in the logs, "k v cache" spelled out, something mis-transcribed in previous tickets. not relevant but FYI.
[00:06:45] Maya Chen: ha, Fireflies strikes again.
[00:06:48] Ethan Park: ok, let's walk through the log snippet you shared. (Ethan shares screen)
[00:07:00] [00:07:12] Ethan Park: here we see allocator spike at t=12.3s, a few transient allocations fail, then a CUDA OOM. after that the runtime tries a single retry, backoff 2s, then second attempt hits OOM again and process restarts. That's why you're seeing the long tail.
[00:07:28] Tom Wu: any kernel-level tuning we can do? like reduce workspace size for attention kernels?
[00:07:33] Oliver Reyes: some kernels expose workspace limits; choosing a different kernel variant (memory-light vs faster) can help. compiler-level flags when building the runtime also affect workspace usage. Redwood's build has profiles; we'll test the "memory-optimized" profile on a repro.
[00:07:48] Raj Patel: what about monitoring signals to detect fragmentation buildup?
[00:07:52] Ethan Park: track reserved vs allocated GPU memory over time, also track free chunks via our allocator metrics. additionally, monitor time-to-first-byte and kernel latency spikes as indirect signs.
[00:08:05] Sarah Lawson: from a compliance side we also need audit logs for retries and fallbacks — does Redwood capture that?
[00:08:10] Maya Chen: yes, audit logs include route-level decisions, retries, fallback events, and allocator OOMs if you enable debug retention. we can increase retention for your account under the enterprise plan.
[00:08:20] Elena Gomez: about VPC/on-prem: if we move to private deployment, will the retry and memory behavior differ?
[00:08:26] Oliver Reyes: behavior can differ because drivers, kernel versions, and node configs are under your control. Private gives you more control to tune drivers, swap, and GC but also more responsibility. we have an on-prem checklist.
[00:08:37] Raj Patel: let's be explicit: best immediate mitigations we can do this week?
[00:08:41] Ethan Park: 1) reduce max_batch to 4 and cap token length to 512 for public-facing routes; 2) enable q4_0 profile in a canary pool for long sequences; 3) set retries=0 for heavy requests or fallback to cached responses; 4) enable allocator async mode; 5) add autoscale threshold earlier.
[00:08:58] Maya Chen: we'll email a config diff for those settings.
[00:09:02] Tom Wu: about the repro harness — how heavy is it and will it interfere with production?
[00:09:06] Oliver Reyes: we'll run it in your test namespace targeting a dedicated pool. it simulates p95 loads and stress patterns. shouldn't touch prod.
[00:09:15] Raj Patel: please make the harness reproduce the KV growth pattern we saw.
[00:09:19] Ethan Park: noted. we'll add a few prompt patterns to emulate rewarm and cold cache cycles.
[00:09:25] Sarah Lawson: any non-obvious gotchas?
[00:09:28] Ethan Park: two gotchas: 1) I/O to host (paging) can cause strange stalls; avoid any host swap; 2) mixed workloads on same GPU (e.g., non-LLM jobs) cause eviction and driver preemption — isolate inference workloads.
[00:09:42] Elena Gomez: we might have some CI jobs that sneak onto those nodes — we'll check node taints.
[00:09:46] Maya Chen: ok folks, to recap: we'll share configs, run the repro, test q4_0, and follow up with a benchmark next Tue. action items are in the notes.
[00:09:58] [00:10:05] Raj Patel: one more question: any recommended observability panels we should add?
[00:10:10] Oliver Reyes: GPU reserved vs allocated, allocator fail counts, KV cache size per model, per-route timeouts and retry counts, and per-host kernel error rates. we'll send a dashboard template.
[00:10:23] Sarah Lawson: thanks team.
[00:10:25] Maya Chen: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the links mentioned. [laughs] and we'll try to keep Fireflies transcription slightly less creative next time.
[00:10:35] [00:10:40] END OF TRANSCRIPT
